newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists demand relaxing Maastricht.
newsitem.headline: French Communists demand relaxing Maastricht.

text.p: France's Communists said they would disclose on Monday a list of demands, including relaxing the Maastricht criteria, made to their Socialist allies in order to take part in a government following the left's election victory.
Pierre Zarka, a member of the Communist Party leadership, said the conditions, drawn from a joint pre-election declaration, also included wage rises and cuts in working hours.
The Communists hold the balance of power in the new National Assembly after the main left-wing Socialist Party failed to win an outright majority.
"We have made precise questions and we expect answers," Zarka told France Inter radio.

"We took them from the joint declaration between the Communist and Socialist parties, including proposals on wages, on reviving consumption, the issue of the 35 hours, how to relax the Maastricht grip so that we no longer suffer external constraints and free ourselves from criteria that are absolutely tragic for the population and the economy," he said.
The left proposed to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 in order to create jobs, and to boost purchasing power in order to trigger a consumer-led economic recovery.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin favours a gradual approach to increasing purchasing power, including through tax reforms, while the Communists call for immediate hikes on low salaries.
"We are not asking for the impossible...We only want universal suffrage to be heard," Zarka said.
"I cannot imagine for a minute that the Socialist Party can turn a deaf ear to the French people's expectations," he added.

The non-Communist left won significantly more seats than the centre-right in the election, but was certain to fall short of an absolute majority in the 577-seat National Assembly, giving the 38 Communist members a potentially pivotal role.

Zarka indicated the Communists were willing to play an active role in a Socialist-led government if they got satisfactory commitments from Socialist leader Lionel Jospin. "Since we want the voice of this country's men and women to be heard in government meetings, we will not be there only as extras," he said.
